summary: A report by J. Pickens at UCSB evaluating ARPANET services from January through March 1972, from a group set up to try out network resources. It reports many unexpected problems, mainly differing software and poor documentation, and gives criteria for ease of use plus suggestions for improvement. It follows on from RFC 302.

eli5.summary: A team tried out all the computers they could reach and wrote down what was hard. Their main complaints were that every machine worked differently and the instructions were poor.

questions: what problems did early arpanet users face
what is friendliness in network services
subtitle: A UCSB graduate seminar tries the early ARPANET as ordinary users and reports what went wrong.

tldr.problem: The early ARPANET offered many resources, but new users struggled to find, reach and use them, and nobody had measured that experience at the user level.
tldr.mechanism: A group of UCSB graduate students explored the network from January to March 1972, answered a questionnaire after nine weeks, graded six sites on reliability, response and friendliness, and proposed fixes.
tldr.outcome: The report blames software heterogeneity and inadequate documentation, defines 'friendliness' as a site criterion, and recommends mini-manuals, better communication among users and a consulting center.

today: RFC 369 is a status Unknown informational report with no listed updates or replacements. It records the user experience of the ARPANET in early 1972 and builds on RFC 302.

sections.title: The Seminar and Its Goals
sections.content:
RFC 369 reports on the group described in RFC 302. It was organized at UCSB from Electrical Engineering graduate students in Computer Science. They knew high level languages and time sharing systems, but no one had experience with the ARPANET.

After two weeks of presentations the group was left to experiment openly. The goal was to learn to use and evaluate network resources, and to be fair but direct about every site, including UCSB. Only five of fourteen students were still active after the first quarter, which the report ties to poor site reliability, few active nodes and hard to find documentation.
sections.eli5: A class learned about a brand new network and then explored it on their own. Many got tired of it because things kept breaking and the instructions were hard to find.

sections.title: What the Survey Measured
sections.content:
Few nodes were active in January to March 1972, so work centered on UCSB, BBN-TENEX, MIT-MULTICS and SRI-ARC, with minor use of HARV-10, UCLA-NMC and UCLA-CCN. Activities included games, text editing, messaging with LINK and SNDMSG, and compiling small programs.

After nine weeks, twelve students answered a questionnaire. On average, users were unable to log into their desired site 35.7% of the time and had trouble free operation 35% of the time. No one put the mean time between failures above two hours, and the average guess was 1 hour. The report itself warns that the questions did not separate node problems from local NCP problems.
sections.eli5: The students said that about a third of the time things just worked. The computers also broke often, usually within an hour or two.

sections.title: Friendliness and Other Complaints
sections.content:
The report offers a definition of friendliness for a site: concise, complete and available documentation, easy system usage, easy to reach help, no message overkill, reasonable reliability and response time, and concise but informative error diagnostics.

The most annoying problem was getting adequate documentation. Similar tasks differed from node to node: editors such as TENEX, TECO, COL and NLS each had their own commands, and each system had its own way to return to the top level. The report also notes inconsistent helpfulness from other researchers, unclear responsibility for network resources, and double connect charges such as $4.00 per hour at UCSB plus $8.00 per hour at BBN-TENEX.
sections.eli5: A friendly computer has clear instructions, easy log in and helpful messages. The students found that every machine did the same job in a different way, which made learning hard.

sections.title: Suggestions and Site Grades
sections.content:
The group still found the network promising, and noted that small problems were fine with current tools. Its suggestions include working groups on problems that need many resources, a short MINIMAN user manual for each site and function, high level subroutine calls to each NCP, a weekly one page network news flier, and a consulting center, perhaps at the NIC. The students also wrote programs for automatic login, file transfer and interprocess communication over TELNET.

Appendix B grades six sites from A to F. BBN-TENEX received A for reliability, response and friendliness, while UCLA-NMC received C-, C and D and MIT-MULTICS received C-, D and C+. The grades are described as subjective.
sections.eli5: The students asked for a short how-to guide for every computer and a help desk. They also gave each computer a school grade.
